draft.title: Judging historical significance
card: Not every event in the past is equally significant. Historians judge significance, which means deciding how much an event matters, using set questions.
Breadth
how many people were affected. An event that changed life for a whole nation is broader than one that touched a single village.
Depth
how strongly people were affected. A change to people's rights, work or survival is deeper than a small change to daily habits.
Duration and relevance
Duration is how long the effects lasted, whether decades or only a year. Relevance is what the event helps explain about today, such as a law, a belief or a conflict that still exists.
draft.remember: Ask how many, how deeply, how long, and what it explains about today.

a.q: Which question is a historian asking when judging the duration of an event's significance?
opts: How long did its effects last?
How many people did it affect?
How strongly did it change lives?
What does it explain about today?
a.why: Duration is about time: how long the effects continued. Asking how many people were affected is breadth, which is easy to confuse with duration because both measure how big the impact was.

b.q: A new law in 1901 changed the rights of one small group of workers in a single town, but the changes it set up shaped their industry for over 80 years. Which judgement fits best?
opts: Narrow in breadth but long in duration
Broad in breadth but short in duration
Narrow in breadth and short in duration
Broad in breadth and long in duration
b.why: Only one small group in a single town was affected, so the breadth is narrow. The effects lasted over 80 years, so the duration is long. The tempting answer is broad and long, but a single town's workers is not a wide number of people.
b.clue: Check the number of people and the length of time separately.

a.best: How long did its effects last?

b.best: Narrow in breadth but long in duration

a.q: A historian argues an event was significant because it took away a group's right to vote, not just their daily habits. Which measure is she using?
opts: Depth
Breadth
Duration
Relevance
a.why: Losing the right to vote is a strong change to people's lives, so she is judging depth. Breadth is tempting, but breadth is about how many people were affected, and she says nothing about numbers.
a.clue: Is she talking about numbers, time, today, or how big the change to lives was?
